extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and researchers of literature; fans of Margaret Atwood
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biographical and bibliographical article summarizing Margaret Atwood's life, career, themes, genres, and reception; useful as a reference for literary study or general information about the author and her works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative fiction vs science fiction (genre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood resists the 'science fiction' label for some works and prefers 'speculative fiction'. She says: 'Science fiction has monsters and spaceships; speculative fiction could really happen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atwood further clarifies: speculative fiction 'employs the means already to hand and ... takes place on Planet Earth.' Science fiction, by her definition, belongs to books with things we can't yet do. Examples cited: The Handmaid's Tale and Oryx and Crake are described as speculative fiction; Oryx and Crake 'contains no intergalactic space travel, no teleportation, no Martians.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility / precedent in speculative fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood asserts a standard of plausibility: 'There's a precedent in real life for everything in the book. I decided not to put anything in that somebody somewhere hadn't already done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard recurs in her later notes (MaddAddam acknowledgements): her fiction 'does not include any technologies or bio-beings that do not already exist, are not under construction or are not possible in theory.' Use this as a criterion when judging speculative worldbuilding — it should be grounded in existing or plausible developments, not entirely fantastical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Canadian identity: survival, victim positions, and garrison mentality
rubrics_metrics.description: In Survival, Atwood postulates that Canadian literature and identity are characterised by the symbol of survival and by frequent use of 'victim positions' (victor/victim relations). She draws on Northrop Frye's concept of 'garrison mentality' — Canada's desire to wall itself off from outside influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these concepts as analytic criteria when reading/teaching Canadian literature: look for recurrent motifs of survival, victimhood, fear of nature, settler history, and community adherence. The 'victor/victim' scale is presented as a tool for interpreting character positions and national literary tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historiographic metafiction (approach to history and narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood's work exemplifies 'historiographic metafiction' — fiction that explicitly explores the relation of history and narrative and the processes of creating history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or teaching texts like The Journals of Susanna Moodie, Alias Grace, The Blind Assassin, and Surfacing, assess how the narrative interrogates historical truth, constructs history, and makes the reader aware of storytelling processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring thematic criteria for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood's works encompass recurring themes: gender and identity, religion and myth, the power of language, climate change, and power politics. Many of her poems are inspired by myths and fairy tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify these themes as primary lenses for critique or close reading. The page lists these themes explicitly and notes their recurrence across poetry, novels, and short fiction — use them to frame thematic essays, course syllabi, or comparative studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feminist criticism focal points
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics often study Atwood's sexual politics, use of myth and fairytale, and gendered relationships — even though Atwood herself sometimes rejects or qualifies the 'feminist' label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical approaches should clarify what is meant by 'feminism' before applying the label. The page notes Atwood's own caution: 'I always want to know what people mean by that word [feminism].' Use sexual politics, mythic structures, and gender dynamics as concrete criteria while avoiding conflation with any single political stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding over-reliance on autobiographical readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood resists critics' tendency to read an author's life too directly into their fiction; filmmakers and critics have found it difficult to locate straightforward autobiographical evidence in her work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting Atwood's texts, be cautious about equating characters/events with the author's biography. The article cites filmmakers' frustration in uncovering autobiographical inspiration as a cautionary example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social science fiction as a subtype descriptor
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood acknowledges that some of her books can be termed 'social science fiction' — works that focus on social, political, or cultural changes rather than speculative technologies beyond current capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label works as social SF when the central speculative element is social organization or societal change (e.g., The Handmaid's Tale, Oryx and Crake). This helps distinguish thematic focus (societal critique) from technocentric science fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding grounded in ethical and real-world issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood's MaddAddam trilogy and Oryx and Crake foreground genetic modification, corporate and pharmaceutical control, and man-made disaster as means to raise ethical questions about science and what it means to be human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realism of ethical concerns and plausible socio-technical dynamics as evaluative criteria for the seriousness and resonance of speculative narratives. The page highlights these specific moral and ecological questions as central to Atwood's speculative project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myth and fairy-tale adaptation/retelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood frequently draws on myths and fairy tales; examples include The Penelopiad (Odyssey retelling) and Hag-Seed (The Tempest retelling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging retellings or mythic adaptations, consider fidelity, inventive perspective (e.g., marginalized voices), and how the retelling interrogates the original's themes. The article notes Atwood's early interest in Grimms' Fairy Tales as formative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation and medium-transfer considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all literary elements translate easily to other media; the Surfacing film 'made little attempt to find cinematic equivalents for the admittedly difficult subjective and poetic dimensions of the novel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting Atwood (or similar literary fiction), assess how subjective voice, poetic language, and interiority will be rendered onscreen or in other formats. Failures to do so are given as an anti-pattern in adaptation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and awards as indicators of reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Atwood's many honours (two Booker Prizes, Arthur C. Clarke Award, Order of Canada, etc.) are listed as measures of critical and institutional recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While awards do not determine literary value alone, they are useful empirical indicators of reception, influence, and standing in literary communities; use them cautiously alongside textual analysis.
